title: US Car Insurance Prices Turned Up in October After a Five-Month Slide
summary: The CPI motor vehicle insurance index rose 0.7% in October after falling about 4.6% from May to September on our calculation, while repair prices kept climbing about 5% to 6% a year, a sign the cheap-renewal window for US drivers may be closing.
description:
For most of 2026, American drivers finally caught a break on car insurance. The government's consumer price index for motor vehicle insurance fell month after month through the spring and summer, after a run of increases that at one point topped 20% a year. The October inflation report, released on November 10, broke that streak: the index rose 0.7% in the month, its second monthly rise in a row and the largest since the decline began in May.

This PolicyRix Team analysis puts the monthly figures together, compares them with repair costs and with what comparison sites report drivers are paying, and explains what it means for renewal season. The monthly changes are from the Bureau of Labor Statistics; the cumulative figures are our own calculations.

The slide and the turn

The seasonally adjusted motor vehicle insurance index fell 1.7% in May, 2.0% in June, 0.3% in July and 0.8% in August, then rose 0.1% in September and 0.7% in October. Chaining those monthly moves together, we calculate that the index fell about 4.6% from the start of May to the end of September. October's rise trims that to a cumulative fall of about 4.0% since May. Over the twelve months to August, the index was down 5.1%, according to BLS data reported by Autobody News.

October's 0.7% may not sound large, but compounded over a year it would be about 8.7%. We are not forecasting that; a single month is noisy and the index has swung both ways in 2026. It does show how quickly the direction can change.

Why repair costs matter

Insurance prices follow claim costs with a lag, and the biggest single driver of claim costs is the price of fixing cars. Those prices did not fall this year. Vehicle maintenance and repair prices rose 5.2% in the twelve months to August, and by September Autobody News reported the measure up 5.8%, with motor vehicle body work up 6.0% over the year. Insurers cut prices in 2025 and early 2026 because they had over-corrected in 2023 and 2024 and had healthy margins to compete with. With repair inflation still running at roughly 5% to 6%, that room shrinks every month.

What drivers are being quoted

Comparison site Insurify, which analyses quotes rather than the CPI, said the national average cost of car insurance held at $143 a month in October. Its mid-year report put the average full-coverage premium at $2,237 a year, up 1% since the end of 2025, after a 6% fall in 2025, and projected $2,242 by the end of 2026. It said 27 states had seen rates rise in the first half. Those figures and the CPI tell a consistent story: the big declines are behind us, and the national average is now roughly flat with pockets of increase.

Insurers' own results point the same way. Liberty Mutual's US retail premiums fell 5.6% in the third quarter, as we reported on November 14, while its underlying combined ratio worsened, which suggests competition and rising costs are squeezing margins at the same time.

What it means for drivers

The practical takeaway is about timing and shopping. Drivers whose policies renew in the next few months are still renewing in a fairly competitive market, so getting two or three comparison quotes is likely to be worth the effort, especially for anyone whose premium jumped in 2023 or 2024 and was never re-shopped. Raising a deductible from $500 to $1,000 can lower the premium, but only makes sense with enough savings to cover the higher amount after an accident. Bundling home and auto, telematics programmes and paying in full can also cut costs, though the savings vary widely by insurer and state.

What the data cannot tell us

The October CPI release could not publish a twelve-month change for motor vehicle insurance, because the Bureau did not collect October 2025 data during the government funding lapse, so we cannot say precisely where prices stand against a year ago. The CPI measures the price of a fixed policy, not what individual households pay after changing cars, drivers or coverage. National averages hide large state differences: Insurify notes that some of the most expensive markets, such as New York and New Jersey, saw premiums fall in the first half while others rose sharply. And one monthly rise does not make a trend; November's CPI, due on December 10, will show whether October was the start of something.

The short version: the cheapest phase of this car insurance cycle may be ending. Repair costs never stopped rising, and October's index suggests insurers are beginning to price that in.
source_name: PolicyRix Team analysis of Bureau of Labor Statistics CPI releases (May to October 2026), Autobody News, Insurify and earlier PolicyRix coverage
image_alt: Driver's hands on a steering wheel at dusk (illustrative)
key_points: The CPI motor vehicle insurance index rose 0.7% in October 2026 after monthly falls of 1.7%, 2.0%, 0.3% and 0.8% from May to August and a 0.1% rise in September.
On our calculation the index fell about 4.6% from May to September and is still about 4.0% lower than at the start of May after October's rise.
Repair prices kept climbing: maintenance and repair was up 5.2% a year in August and 5.8% in September, with body work up 6.0%.
Insurify put the national average at $143 a month in October and projects full coverage at $2,242 a year by the end of 2026, up about 1%.
BLS could not publish an October twelve-month change because October 2025 data were not collected; the November CPI is due December 10.
why_it_matters: Car insurance is one of the largest fixed costs for US households. The October turn in the price index, with repair costs still rising, suggests the window of falling renewals may be closing, so drivers renewing soon have a stronger reason to compare quotes now.

title: India's Big Four Life Insurers: Who Made More From New Business in H1
summary: A PolicyRix Team scorecard of LIC, SBI Life, HDFC Life and ICICI Life for the first half of FY27 finds their combined value of new business rose about 25% to Rs 13,436 crore, but LIC's jump came almost entirely from a wider margin rather than more sales.
description:
India's four largest listed life insurers have now all reported results for the six months to September 30, 2026, and putting them side by side shows two very different ways to grow profits from new policies. The private insurers mostly grew by selling more. LIC, the state-owned market leader, grew by making each sale more profitable.

This PolicyRix Team analysis compares value of new business, or VNB, which estimates the present value of future profits from policies sold in the period, and the VNB margin, which divides that by annualised premium equivalent, or APE, a standard measure of new sales. The company figures come from their results as covered in our earlier stories and from reporting on LIC's results of November 5. The shares, decompositions and checks are our own calculations.

The scorecard

LIC: VNB of Rs 6,846 crore, up about 34% from Rs 5,111 crore, on APE of Rs 30,696 crore, up 5.7%. Net VNB margin 22.3%, up from 17.6%. Half-year standalone profit Rs 25,568 crore, up 21.5%.

SBI Life: VNB of Rs 3,270 crore, up 19%, on APE of Rs 11,750 crore, up 18%. Reported margin 27.9%; dividing VNB by APE gives 27.8%. Half-year profit Rs 1,270 crore, up 17%.

HDFC Life: VNB of Rs 2,037 crore, up 12%, on APE of Rs 8,245 crore, up 11%. Margin 24.7%, against 24.5%. Half-year profit Rs 1,119 crore, up about 13%.

ICICI Life, formerly ICICI Prudential Life: VNB of Rs 1,283 crore, up 22.3%, on APE of about Rs 4,935 crore, up 15.1%. Margin 26.0%, against 24.7%. Half-year profit Rs 760 crore, up 26.5%.

Together, on our calculation, the four generated Rs 13,436 crore of VNB, up about 25% from Rs 10,728 crore, on combined APE of about Rs 55,626 crore. Their blended margin was about 24.2%.

Volume or margin?

VNB growth can be split into two parts: growth in sales and change in margin. On our calculation, LIC's VNB rose about 34% while its APE rose under 6%, which means roughly 27% of the improvement came from the higher margin. For SBI Life and HDFC Life, the margin effect was below 1%; nearly all their VNB growth came from selling more. ICICI Life sat between the two, with about 6% from margin and the rest from volume. Excluding LIC, the three private insurers' combined VNB grew about 17%.

LIC's market weight explains why its margin matters so much. It generated about 51% of the four insurers' combined VNB with about 55% of their APE, on our calculation, so its lower margin than the private players still drags the blended figure down, but by less each year.

Why the margins differ

VNB margins reflect product mix. Protection policies, which pay out on death or illness, and guaranteed non-participating savings products tend to carry higher margins than participating policies and unit-linked plans. Analysts covering ICICI Life said a higher share of lower-margin group funds weighed on its second-quarter margin, even as retail protection grew. LIC has said its improvement comes from product diversification and distribution, and reports describe a shift toward non-participating products. HDFC Life's stable margin, as we noted in October, suggests little change in mix.

What it means for policyholders

A higher VNB margin means an insurer expects to earn more profit from each rupee of new premium. That is good for shareholders, but it says nothing about whether a particular policy is good value for the buyer. For customers, the questions are the same as ever: whether a pure term plan meets the protection need more cheaply than a savings-linked product, what the surrender value is in the early years, and how the insurer handles claims. Persistency, the share of customers still paying after one or five years, is a useful signal of whether products were sold to people who wanted them. It is also worth watching IRDAI's proposed limits on expenses and commissions, which HDFC Life's management flagged as a near-term friction and which could change how products are priced and sold.

What the data cannot tell us

The companies do not all calculate VNB on identical assumptions, so margins are not perfectly comparable. LIC's VNB is struck on a net basis that may differ from private insurers' methods. Half-year figures can swing with large group deals. We do not have product-level splits for all four, so our explanation of margin differences relies on company and analyst commentary. Profit figures under Indian accounting rules are not directly comparable with VNB and say little about long-term value.

The headline is that India's life insurance profitability rose sharply in the first half, but LIC's rise came from pricing and mix while the private insurers mostly had to sell more to grow.
source_name: PolicyRix Team analysis of H1 FY27 results from LIC, SBI Life, HDFC Life and ICICI Life, using Free Press Journal, PSU Watch, Kotak Neo, Upstox and earlier PolicyRix coverage
key_points: LIC's H1 FY27 VNB rose about 34% to Rs 6,846 crore and its net VNB margin widened to 22.3% from 17.6%, while its APE grew only 5.7%.
SBI Life's VNB rose 19% to Rs 3,270 crore, HDFC Life's 12% to Rs 2,037 crore and ICICI Life's 22.3% to Rs 1,283 crore.
On our calculation the four insurers' combined VNB rose about 25% to Rs 13,436 crore at a blended margin of about 24.2%.
About 27% of LIC's VNB growth came from margin, while SBI Life's and HDFC Life's growth came almost entirely from higher sales.
Margins measure profit for the insurer, not value for the buyer; persistency and IRDAI's proposed expense limits are the items to watch.
why_it_matters: These four insurers sell most of India's life cover. Whether they grow by selling more or by earning more per policy shapes the products agents and banks push, so buyers should judge policies on their own needs and costs rather than on the insurer's margins.

title: Lemonade, Root, Hippo: Three Insurtechs, Three Paths in Q3
summary: A PolicyRix Team comparison of Lemonade, Root and Hippo's third quarters shows Root shrinking premium to stay profitable, Hippo growing 60% while keeping only about 30% of the risk, and Lemonade growing 34% while still losing money, as it keeps more risk for itself.
description:
Five years after the big insurtech listings, the three best-known US digital insurers have settled on very different strategies, and their third-quarter 2026 results make the contrast unusually clear. One is giving up growth to protect profit, one is growing fast by passing most of its risk to others, and one is growing fast while taking on more risk and still losing money.

This PolicyRix Team analysis compares Lemonade, Root and Hippo using figures from their third-quarter results, as covered in our earlier stories and in reporting by Reinsurance News and Insurance Business. The ratios and changes marked as ours are our own calculations.

Root: profit by shrinking

Root, which sells car insurance, reported net income of $14.4 million against a loss a year earlier. Its gross combined ratio improved to 96.8% from 101.3%, meaning it now earns more in premium than it pays in claims and costs. But gross written premium fell 8% to $357.5 million, even though policies in force rose 4% to 484,037. On our calculation, premium per policy fell about 8.9%, to $1,441 from $1,581. The company said it deliberately gave up growth in its direct channel where expected returns fell below its threshold, and it has leaned on partners such as Carvana.

Hippo: growth with low retention

Hippo grew gross written premium 60% to $498 million and reported a combined ratio of 98.4%, against 99.6%. It also raised its full-year guidance. But net written premium, what it keeps after reinsurance, rose only 26% to $149 million. On our calculation, it retained about 30% of what it wrote, down from 38%. Hippo has also moved away from its roots: casualty business grew 146% and made up 38% of gross premium, while homeowners fell to 23%. Net income was $9 million.

Lemonade: growth while taking back risk

Lemonade's in-force premium rose 34% to $1.55 billion and revenue jumped 73% to $336.1 million. Most of the revenue jump came from keeping more of its own business: ceded earned premium, the share passed to reinsurers, fell to $69.3 million from $134.7 million, according to Reinsurance News, a drop of about 49% on our calculation. That means Lemonade now carries more of its own losses. The gross loss ratio rose to 65% from 62%, and to 63% from 56% excluding catastrophes. The net loss widened to $43.7 million, about 13% of revenue on our calculation, though adjusted EBITDA losses narrowed and the company guided to its first positive adjusted EBITDA quarter in the fourth quarter. Shares fell about 7% on the day of the results, according to Insurance Business.

What the three paths tell us

Our reading is that each company is answering the same question, how to make a digital insurer profitable, in a different way. Root is pricing for margin and accepting slower growth, which is the conventional insurance answer in a competitive car market. Hippo is acting partly like a platform, writing business and passing much of the risk to reinsurers and partners, which reduces volatility but also caps how much underwriting profit it keeps. Lemonade is betting that its pricing models are good enough to keep more risk, which raises both the potential reward and the exposure to bad quarters, such as the higher loss ratio this time.

What it means for customers

For car insurance buyers, Root's falling premium per policy is consistent with the broader softening in auto pricing this year, and with growth through partners that may offer quotes at the point of buying a car. For Lemonade customers, management said on its earnings call that it is taking rate increases where claim costs have risen, including pet insurance, which is now its largest line, so some renewals may cost more. For Hippo homeowners, the shift toward commercial and casualty lines does not change existing policies, but it shows where the company sees its future. In all three cases, policies are backed by licensed insurance carriers, and state insurance regulators oversee their solvency.

What the data cannot tell us

The three companies define key measures differently: Root reports gross and net combined ratios, Hippo a single combined ratio, and Lemonade loss ratios and adjusted EBITDA rather than a combined ratio. Their lines of business differ, so their ratios are not directly comparable. One quarter can be distorted by catastrophe losses or reinsurance changes, and Lemonade's investor day on November 17 may add new targets.

The headline is that the insurtechs are no longer judged only on growth. Root is profitable but smaller, Hippo is growing with others' capital, and Lemonade is still paying for scale.
source_name: PolicyRix Team analysis of third-quarter 2026 results from Lemonade, Root and Hippo, using Reinsurance News, Insurance Business and earlier PolicyRix coverage
image_alt: Analytics dashboard on a laptop screen (illustrative)
key_points: Root earned $14.4 million with a 96.8% gross combined ratio, but gross written premium fell 8% and premium per policy fell about 8.9% to $1,441 on our calculation.
Hippo grew gross written premium 60% to $498 million with a 98.4% combined ratio, while keeping only about 30% of what it wrote, down from 38%.
Lemonade's in-force premium rose 34% to $1.55 billion and revenue 73%, helped by cutting ceded premium about 49%, but its net loss widened to $43.7 million.
Lemonade's gross loss ratio rose to 65% from 62%, and to 63% from 56% excluding catastrophes, as it kept more of its own risk.
The companies report different measures and lines, so their ratios are not directly comparable.
why_it_matters: Digital insurers now cover millions of US renters, drivers, pet owners and homeowners. How each balances growth, profit and risk shapes their pricing and stability, which matters to customers choosing between them and established carriers.

title: UK Car Finance: FCA Sets Rules for Early Compensation Offers
summary: The FCA said on November 3 that lenders may make early car finance compensation offers while its redress scheme is partly suspended, but each offer must be at least the maximum the scheme would pay; Barclays Partner Finance is so far the only lender taking part.
description:
Millions of UK drivers waiting for car finance compensation have a new route to getting paid sooner, but only if their lender chooses to offer it. On November 3, the Financial Conduct Authority set out minimum standards for voluntary early settlement offers that lenders can make while its industry-wide redress scheme is partly suspended by a legal challenge. The key rule is simple: an early offer must be no less than the maximum compensation the customer could get under the scheme.

This article is based on the FCA's statements on the scheme and reporting by Securities.io and Lanop.

Why compensation has stalled

The FCA confirmed its motor finance redress scheme in March 2026 to compensate people who were not told about commission arrangements when they bought a car on finance. It covers regulated agreements taken out between April 6, 2007 and November 1, 2024. According to Securities.io, the FCA estimates about 37% of agreements in that period are eligible, about 12.1 million, with an average payout of around 830 pounds per agreement. Payments were due to start in 2026.

In July, the Upper Tribunal partly suspended the scheme after challenges by Consumer Voice and several motor finance lenders, including Volkswagen Financial Services, Mercedes-Benz Financial Services and Credit Agricole Auto Finance. Lenders no longer have to calculate or pay compensation on the scheme timetable until the legal process ends. The FCA's July statement gave hearing dates of December 14 to 18, 2026 or February 16 to 26, 2027; Securities.io reports the hearing is now scheduled for February 16 to March 3, 2027. If the scheme is upheld and not appealed, the FCA expects payments to begin in 2027. If it is overturned in whole or part, compensation could slip to 2028 or later.

What the new rules say

Lenders are not required to make early offers and can limit them to some customers. Where they do, the FCA expects that:

the offer is at least the maximum redress the customer could receive under the scheme;
customers get at least one month to decide;
letters do not suggest the FCA has approved the individual offer;
an appendix explains the arrangements found and how the amount was calculated, including any caps, interest and tax deduction;
lenders include the FCA's consumer factsheet and tell the FCA they are taking part.

Barclays Partner Finance is the first, and so far only, lender on the FCA's list of participating firms. Lanop reports it plans offers to selected customers whose complaints it acknowledged by October 1, 2026.

The trade-off for customers

Accepting an early offer is full and final for issues within the scheme. Customers keep the money even if the legal challenge later reduces what the scheme would pay, but they cannot claim more if the outcome is better. The offer itself cannot be referred to the Financial Ombudsman Service; a customer who disagrees can reject it and wait for the scheme. Separate complaints, for example about GAP insurance or affordability, must be dealt with separately. The FCA's general counsel, Stephen Braviner Roman, said fair settlement offers could get some people money sooner. In a Kantar survey for the FCA, 89% of complainants said they wanted the choice of an offer now.

What borrowers should do

People who bought a car on finance between 2007 and 2024 can complain to their lender directly and for free; the FCA warns that some claims firms and law firms charge more than 30% of any compensation. Anyone who receives an early offer should check that the appendix shows the calculation and compare it with the FCA's factsheet before deciding. The FCA says lenders should tell complainants who are not owed money by November 18, 2026, if their agreement started on or after April 1, 2014 and they complained by June 30, 2026. Borrowers should also watch for scams; the FCA lists genuine lender contact details on its website.

What we do not know

It is not clear how many lenders will follow Barclays, or how many customers will receive offers. The outcome of the tribunal hearing will decide whether the scheme stands as designed. Estimates of the total industry cost vary between reports, and the FCA's figures may change if the scheme is altered.
source_name: Financial Conduct Authority statements on the motor finance redress scheme (July and November 2026), Securities.io and Lanop
image_alt: A white SUV parked on a wet road near mountains (illustrative)
key_points: On November 3, the FCA said early car finance offers must be no less than the maximum redress a customer could get under its partly suspended scheme.
Customers must get at least one month to decide; accepting is full and final, and the offer cannot be referred to the Financial Ombudsman Service.
Barclays Partner Finance is the only lender on the FCA's participating list so far.
The scheme covers agreements from April 6, 2007 to November 1, 2024; the FCA estimates about 12.1 million eligible agreements and an average of about 830 pounds each.
The legal challenge is due to be heard in early 2027; the FCA expects payments in 2027 if the scheme is upheld, or 2028 or later if not.
why_it_matters: Millions of UK drivers are owed compensation for undisclosed car finance commission, but payouts are stuck behind a legal challenge. Early offers could mean money sooner for some, but accepting one is final, so borrowers need to check the calculation carefully.

title: Hiscox Grows Premiums 9.5% as Its UK Small-Business Arm Speeds Up
summary: Hiscox's insurance contract written premiums rose 9.5% to $4.44 billion in the first nine months of 2026, led by retail and an 11.1% rise in its UK business, while rates fell 5% in its London market arm and 14% in reinsurance.
description:
Specialist insurer Hiscox, best known in the UK for small business and home insurance, reported faster growth in the first nine months of 2026 even as prices in its larger-risk businesses kept falling. Group insurance contract written premiums rose 9.5% to 4.44 billion US dollars, up from 4.05 billion, or 8.1% at constant currency, in a trading statement published on November 3.

This article draws on the company's statement as reported by AJ Bell and Alliance News, Reinsurance News, Insurance Times and Marketbeat's summary of the analyst call.

What changed

The growth came mostly from Hiscox Retail, which sells to small businesses and wealthy households. Retail premiums rose 12% to 2.25 billion dollars, or 9.1% at constant currency, with double-digit growth in the third quarter. Hiscox UK grew 11.1% at constant currency to 811.1 million dollars, according to Reinsurance News; Insurance Times put the UK figure at 603.1 million pounds, up from 543.1 million. Hiscox said the UK growth was driven by volume rather than price, with retail rates up only 1%, and by its digital direct business for smaller companies, where new business rose about 40%.

The big-ticket side looked different. In the London Market division, which covers larger and specialist risks, premiums rose 9.9% to about 1.05 billion dollars, but rates fell 5% over nine months. Hiscox said they remain 59% above 2018 levels. In reinsurance, gross premiums rose 4.5% to 1.13 billion dollars, but net premiums, what Hiscox keeps after passing risk to third-party capital, fell 7.5% to 486 million dollars, and rates fell 14%. The company said it cut catastrophe exposure and used more outside capital as prices softened. Assets under management in its insurance-linked securities business reached a record, according to Marketbeat.

Claims and investments

Hiscox said claims in the third quarter were within expectations, with few natural catastrophes offsetting shipping losses linked to conflict in the Middle East, AJ Bell reported. The investment result for nine months was 104.2 million dollars, a 1.2% return, down from 350.8 million dollars a year earlier. The company said its reinvestment yield rose to 5.1% from 4.4% at the half year as bond yields increased. Hiscox kept its target of about 9% constant currency growth in retail for the full year.

How it compares with last year

The pace has picked up. A year ago, Hiscox reported nine-month premium growth of 5.9% to 4.05 billion dollars, with retail up 6.1% at constant currency and retail rates up 2%. This year's 9.5% group growth and 9.1% retail growth came with retail rates up only about 1%, which on our reading means almost all of the acceleration came from selling more policies rather than charging more. In the United States, Hiscox's premiums rose 8.4% to 791.6 million dollars, according to Coverager, which also reported that the company has started advertising inside an AI chatbot as part of its push into online sales.

What it means for policyholders

For small businesses, the results show a large specialist insurer competing hard for customers rather than pushing up prices: retail growth came from more policies, and retail rates rose only about 1%. That usually means renewal increases should be modest for clean risks, and buying online is getting easier as Hiscox and rivals expand digital channels. Small business owners can use that competition to compare cover, especially for professional indemnity, public liability and cyber, where policy wordings differ significantly.

For larger buyers, falling rates in the London Market point to more favourable renewals, especially in property, though the company said it is walking away from business it considers under-priced. In reinsurance, falling prices fit the broader picture from this year's results, as we reported in our November 14 analysis of catastrophe budgets.

What we do not know

The statement is a trading update, so it does not include a combined ratio or profit for the nine months; full-year results are due early next year. Exchange rate movements flatter dollar-reported UK figures, which is why the constant currency numbers differ. The company did not quantify the Middle East shipping losses in the reports we reviewed.
source_name: Hiscox Ltd Q3 2026 trading statement (November 3, 2026), via AJ Bell/Alliance News, Reinsurance News, Insurance Times and Marketbeat
key_points: Hiscox's insurance contract written premiums rose 9.5% to $4.44 billion in the first nine months of 2026, or 8.1% at constant currency.
Retail premiums rose 9.1% at constant currency to $2.25 billion, and Hiscox UK grew 11.1%, driven by volume with retail rates up about 1%.
London Market rates fell 5% but remain 59% above 2018 levels; reinsurance rates fell 14% and net reinsurance premiums fell 7.5% to $486 million.
The nine-month investment result fell to $104.2 million, a 1.2% return, from $350.8 million, though the reinvestment yield rose to 5.1%.
Third-quarter claims were within expectations, with few catastrophes offsetting Middle East shipping losses.
why_it_matters: Hiscox is a major insurer of UK small businesses and high-value homes. Growth driven by volume rather than price points to a competitive market where small firms can expect modest renewals and should compare cover, while larger buyers benefit from falling specialist rates.

title: Great Eastern Q3 Profit Falls 72% as Investments Drag, Core Grows
summary: Great Eastern's third-quarter net profit fell 72% to S$102.9 million on investment losses and the sale of its Indonesian unit, but core insurance profit rose 6% and new business value grew 14%, and nine-month profit was almost flat at S$952.4 million.
description:
Great Eastern Holdings, one of Singapore's largest life insurers and a subsidiary of OCBC, reported a sharp fall in third-quarter profit as weaker investment results hit both its insurance fund and its shareholders' fund. Net profit for the quarter to September 30 was S$102.9 million, down 72% from S$372.0 million a year earlier. The underlying insurance business kept growing, however, and nine-month profit was only 1% lower.

The results were published on November 2. This article is based on reporting by RecordOwl, which cites the company's SGX release, and on OCBC's third-quarter results statement of November 6.

What changed

The swing came from investments. Investment profit in the insurance fund turned to a loss of S$30.8 million from a gain of S$59.6 million, and the shareholders' fund recorded a loss of S$45.6 million against a profit of S$143.2 million a year earlier. As a result, profit from the insurance business fell 35% to S$148.5 million. OCBC, which owns Great Eastern, said its own insurance income fell 37% in the quarter, mainly reflecting Great Eastern's weaker investment performance.

The quarter was also affected by the sale of Great Eastern's Indonesian life business, which closed on September 1 so the group could comply with Indonesian ownership rules, according to RecordOwl.

Core business still grew

Core insurance profit, which excludes investment swings, rose 6% to S$179.3 million from S$169.2 million. New business embedded value, or NBEV, the estimated value of profits from policies sold in the period, rose 14% to S$208.2 million from S$182.2 million. OCBC said NBEV and margins continued to grow with a favourable product mix.

For the first nine months, net profit was S$952.4 million, 1% below S$965.7 million a year earlier. Total weighted new sales rose 9% to S$1,175.6 million, NBEV rose 23% to S$613.5 million, and core insurance profit rose 22% to S$742.7 million. On our calculation, that means core insurance profit made up about 78% of nine-month net profit, against about 63% a year earlier, so earnings now depend less on investment gains.

OCBC reported that Great Eastern's nine-month profit contribution to the group rose 5% to S$941 million.

How the year has unfolded

The third quarter stands out against a strong first half. In the first quarter, Great Eastern reported profit of S$346.3 million, roughly unchanged, with weighted new sales up 16% and NBEV up 31%, led by Singapore. For the first half, profit attributable to shareholders rose 43% to S$849.5 million and NBEV rose 28% to S$405.3 million, helped by strong investment results. On our calculation, the nine-month profit of S$952.4 million less the first-half figure gives the S$102.9 million third-quarter result, so the whole year-on-year decline in nine-month profit came in one quarter. For context, the group reported a record full-year profit of S$1,207.1 million for 2025, with NBEV up 19%.

What it means for policyholders

For Great Eastern's policyholders, a quarterly fall in reported profit caused by market movements does not by itself affect their policies. Guaranteed benefits are backed by the insurer's capital, which in Singapore is supervised by the Monetary Authority of Singapore under risk-based capital rules. The more relevant figures for customers are the growth in new business, which suggests products are selling well, and the investment results in the participating fund, because bonuses on participating, or with-profits, policies depend partly on how those investments perform over time. A single weak quarter rarely changes bonus rates, which insurers smooth over years, but policyholders with participating plans can check the annual bonus declarations and the projected rates in their policy illustrations.

What we do not know

The reports we reviewed do not give a capital adequacy ratio for the quarter or break down which investments caused the losses. The figures for the Indonesian unit before and after the sale are not separated in the summary data. We relied on one detailed report of the company's release plus OCBC's statement; readers wanting the full detail should consult the company's SGX filing.
source_name: Great Eastern Holdings 9M-26 results (November 2, 2026) as reported by RecordOwl, and OCBC Group third-quarter 2026 results (November 6, 2026)
image_alt: Singapore skyline representing the city's financial and insurance sector (illustrative)
key_points: Great Eastern's third-quarter net profit fell 72% to S$102.9 million from S$372.0 million, as investment results in both the insurance and shareholders' funds turned negative.
Core insurance profit rose 6% to S$179.3 million and NBEV rose 14% to S$208.2 million in the quarter.
Nine-month net profit was S$952.4 million, down 1%, while NBEV rose 23% to S$613.5 million and core insurance profit rose 22% to S$742.7 million.
On our calculation, core insurance profit was about 78% of nine-month net profit, up from about 63% a year earlier.
OCBC said its insurance income fell 37% in the quarter mainly because of Great Eastern's weaker investment performance.
why_it_matters: Great Eastern insures millions of people in Singapore and Malaysia. A profit fall driven by investment swings does not affect guaranteed benefits, but investment returns in the participating fund feed into bonuses over time, which matters to holders of with-profits policies.
